rv.q: Having Fleming herself belt out notes - and self-pompously believe her voice has the ability to cure the disabled - is delicious.
It’s all shamelessly silly, and it works: In Joe DiPietro’s play, based on Garson Kanin’s 1985 “Peccadillo,” broad jokes and shameless hamming make for a guilty pleasure.
But the show doesn’t play as amusingly as it should because the young ghostwriters aren’t the perfect match they’re meant to be.
The glimpse of real grandeur in that voice makes this trifle of a play seem even smaller.
Fleming’s stage persona is too wholesome to make us believe fully her flights of temperament.
There is something almost daring about Broadway's inexplicable insistence on throwback fluff-ball comedies this spring.
But on Broadway, it's piffle, forgotten by the time you reach the corner.
Would that the play achieved that tricky balance with such panache.
It may have been the only genuine laugh of the night.
Living on Love is meant to be hammy, but it’s not even that. It’s a bland, synthetic dud: a ham-flavored turkey.
It's so unfunny as to make the viewer despair of ever laughing again, much as a starving man might despair of ever eating again.

When: On sale through Aug. 2.Show times vary. How much: $25-$145, call (212) 239-6200 or visit telecharge.com With a pooch named Puccini, a full operatic costume in her closet and servants who are perfectly willing to create a snowy scene in her living room, it's safe to say that Angelis is a woman at the height of divadom.

With all due respect to the diva of the hour, the real revelation of “Living on Love” is Sills, whose divo Vito enters the Broadway pantheon of great, inspired, and completely over the-top comic creations.
Sills, of Broadway’s “The Scarlet Pimpernel” and “Little Shop…,” is a comic marvel as the out-of-tune conductor who thinks he still has a way with the ladies.
He's fashioned an entirely serviceable screwball comedy for the occasion: lighthearted, lightweight and with a dollop of sentimentality.
Here, at least, they make for lively company — even when saddled with lackluster material.
DiPietro cannot decide if he is the Marx Brothers, Abbot and Costello or Dashiell Hammett, so his writing ends up with no flavor of his own.
“Living on Love” might have been enjoyable were it not for the complete emptiness of the piece itself.
What you get when you cross this crossed Private Lives and Kiss Me, Kate are a few moments of bland silliness.
But too many lame jokes and broad-as-a-barn performances extinguish any chance of that, in a production directed by Kathleen Marshall.

cn.t: Critics find this frothy comedy a mediocre vehicle for Fleming's Broadway debut, with mixed praise for her game performance but widespread criticism of DiPietro's thin, clichéd material and old-fashioned fluff.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.vl: Skip for any show with detail
sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
